title: Arp 107 composite image (NIRCam + MIRI)
caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 107, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: Arp 107 · constellation Leo Minor · about 465 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #57 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A larger galaxy, just right of centre, has a hazy white core and a ring of red and orange gaseous filaments, with a noticeable gap at the top left edged by two big orange pockets of dust and gas. A smaller, hazy white galaxy sits beside it. This is Arp 107, a pair about 465 million light-years away, seen by Webb's NIRCam and MIRI.

The two galaxies collided hundreds of millions of years ago. In near-infrared light, shown in white, older stars shine brightly in both, along with a faint bridge of gas stretching between them. Background galaxies glow vividly at these wavelengths too.

MIRI's mid-infrared data show young stars and star-forming regions in orange and red, and give the clearest view of the point of impact, marked by the gap at the top of the spiral. The crash set off a fresh round of star birth and also produced what looks like a smile.
scale: The source lists a distance of 465 million light years, so the light in this picture set out roughly 465 million years ago.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam near-infrared data appear in white, and MIRI's mid-infrared data appear in orange and red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye.
